title: The checkout that watches back
text: The self-checkout was sold as convenience and {{1}} as surveillance. Retailers introduced the machines to {{2}} labour costs; customers accepted them for shorter queues; and everyone quickly discovered the {{3}}: with no cashier watching, some shoppers scan nothing at all, others {{4}} expensive items as cheap ones, and the machines must therefore {{5}} every movement — weighing unexpected items, pausing for attendant approval, {{6}} cameras at the basket. The result is a compromise nobody designed. Honest shoppers {{7}} the nagging — 'unexpected item in the bagging area' — retailers accept a level of loss they quietly price into the goods, and the industry keeps {{8}} with better cameras and computer vision that recognises a banana without a barcode. Economists call it shrinkage management; shoppers call it being distrusted by a machine. The till, meanwhile, has quietly become one of the most sophisticated computer-vision laboratories most people will ever stand inside.

gaps.explanation: 'sold as convenience and received as surveillance' — the parallel of selling and receiving; recoup = recover a loss.
'to trim labour costs' — cut them back neatly; triple = multiply by three, the opposite direction.
'everyone discovered the flaw' — the weakness in the arrangement; fringe = an edge.
'log expensive items as cheap ones' — record them dishonestly; lug = carry heavily.
'the machines must monitor every movement' — keep watch on it; muster = gather (courage).
'angling cameras at the basket' — pointing them obliquely at it; anchor = fix firmly in place.
'honest shoppers overlook the nagging' — tolerate and ignore it; overrule = reverse a decision.
'the industry keeps experimenting with better cameras' — 'experiment with' is the fixed pattern; exonerate = clear of blame.
